Many soybean fields in west
ern Ohio are beginning to show
signs of manganese deficiency.
Those fields likely will yield
fewer beans this fall unless they
are treated, says Dale Friday,
Ohio State University extension
agronomist.


Manganese deficiency shows
up as light green mottling on
the leaves. AS the plants con-
tinue to grow, the light-colored
patches become yellow and
more noticeable. In severe cases
and in late stages of plant
development, the yellow patches
of tissue die and become brown.


Symptoms of manganese de-
ficiency are more widespread
this year than last, Friday says.
The cool weather of mid-June
probably has made the deficiency
more pronounced than it would
have been in a normal growing
season, the agronomist points
out. Symptoms are more notice
able in low spots, tending to
taper off at the edges of such
areas.


Correcting the deficiency is
neither difficult nor expensive,
Friday says, and it can mean
several more bushels of beans
per acre. In Ohio Agricultural
Experiment Station tests, treat
ment has boosted yield from five
to Is bushels an acre. This re-
commended treatment is to spray
the beans with 5 to 10 pounds
per acre of manganese sulfate in
10 to 20 gallons of water.
Most Ohio soils, Friday ex-
plains, contain enough manganese
for normal crop growth. 1t is
generally in western Ohio that
the deficiency is a problem.
